title: Was Cao Chong's Elephant Story Fake? Sun Quan Had None Till 210; a Sutra Has It Too
description:
You surely know how Cao Chong weighed the elephant. But the same trick (put the elephant on a boat, mark the waterline, then weigh goods loaded to that mark) is also in a Buddhist sutra translated in the Northern Wei, the Za Baozang Jing, in its Tale of the Land That Casts Out the Old, and the one who solves it is an old man hidden in an underground room.

The doubts, in the order they grew: the passage in Chen Shou's main text of the Records of the Three Kingdoms (it opens with one word, shi, "at that time": no year, no stones, no age for Cao Chong that year; Pei Songzhi added no note); the two years the Qing scholar He Zhuo set side by side: the Records has Cao Chong die in Jian'an 13 (208), another eulogy says Jian'an 12 (207), and Sun Quan took elephant-rich Jiaozhou only in Jian'an 15 (210), so "this story was embellished"; Shao Jinhan's precedent, a huge pig weighed by boat in the Fuzi; Chen Yinke's 1930 article in the Tsinghua Journal and his verdict, and the sutra's translation, made only in 472, 175 years after Chen Shou died; and the other side's records: the "two tame elephants" from Sun Quan in Cao Pi's Letter to Wang Lang, the two tame elephants sent to Liu Shan, the tame elephant kept at the Jin court, and the "still young" in Yu Pu's Jiangbiao Zhuan. Who thought of it first, no document settles: this file is open.

Histories: the Wenyuange Siku Quanshu Records (with Pei Songzhi's notes and collation) and the Book of Jin; the lost Jiangbiao Zhuan, Letter to Wang Lang, Fuzi, Eulogy for Cangshu and Jin Zhugong Zan via the Yiwen Leiju, Chuxue Ji and Taiping Yulan; the sutra: CBETA Taisho T0203 and the Chu Sanzang Jiji; Chen Yinke: scans of the Tsinghua Journal 6.1 (June 1930), pp. 17-20, whose contents page says "Indian tales" for "Buddhist tales." Lines saying "we think" are this channel's view. We discuss only where the texts come from, not any faith.

Illustrations are AI-generated; historical figures are unnamed cartoons, not likenesses.

Data as of 2026-10-19 (rewritten 2026-10-25 under new rules)

ce101.text: You surely know Cao Chong weighing the elephant: the textbook genius.

ce102.text: But this story, in histories for over 1,700 years, has a piece that doesn't fit.

ce103.text: In the Jian'an era, Sun Quan sent a giant elephant.

ce104.text: Cao Cao wanted its weight, but none of his men could tell.

ce105.text: Young Cao Chong said: put it on a big boat, mark the waterline.

ce106.text: Then weigh goods loaded to that mark. Delighted, Cao Cao did just that.

ce107.text: Chen Shou, who wrote this, dates the elephant with one word, shi: "then." The year? Not given.

ce108.text: But that's not the oddest part. A Qing man ran the numbers on it.

ce109.text: Years later there's also a letter mentioning two tame elephants. Who wrote it?

ce110.text: This file follows that carved mark from the Three Kingdoms to 1930.

ce111.text: Who first thought of the boat mark?

ce200.text: Who thought of it first? Check who wrote it first.

ce201.text: Chen Shou, who wrote Cao Chong's passage, was a Jin man who died in 297; the book was done before.

ce202.text: And it's in his main text, not a later note: Chen Shou wrote it himself.

ce202b.text: Open the Records of the Three Kingdoms: Chen Shou's main text, and notes added later.

ce204.text: Chen Shou wrote: a bright child, at five or six he had an adult's mind.

ce205.text: The weighing follows, but his age that year? Not written.

ce206.text: Your "weighed it at five or six" came from later readers.

ce207.text: And that opening "weigh goods": Chen Shou never says what goods.

ce208.text: In your version, did the boat carry stones?

ce209.text: Honestly, the first time I read the original, I froze too: our version has extras Chen Shou never wrote.

ce210.text: Pei Songzhi, who later added notes, presented them to the court in 429.

ce211.text: He added not one note here, only faulting another book's style. No sign of doubt.

ce212.text: The year Cao Chong died, though, Chen Shou spells out. Which year?

ce301.text: In the 13th year of Jian'an, 208, Cao Chong fell ill at age 13.

ce302.text: Cao Cao prayed for him in person, yet lost him.

ce303.text: But another eulogy for him puts it a year earlier, Jian'an 12, also saying he died at 13.

ce304.text: Per the Records, that same year Sun Quan and Liu Bei crushed Cao Cao at Red Cliffs.

ce305.text: Cao Cao's records are brief: it went badly, plague struck the army, many died, he withdrew.

ce306.text: Then open war; 9 years on, Sun Quan asked to submit.

ce307.text: So when did Sun Quan send the elephant?

ce308.text: Southern Song scholar Ye Shi wrote four characters on it: gai tian bing ye, meaning the boy was born gifted.

ce310.text: The Qing man who ran the numbers was the scholar He Zhuo. Doubting it, he found two years. Which?

ce311.text: In 200, Sun Ce died and Sun Quan had just taken over; Cao Cao even petitioned to make him a general.

ce312.text: In 210, Sun Quan sent a man to be inspector of Jiaozhou, and only then did it obey him. Why Jiaozhou?

ce313.text: Because its south, Jiuzhen and Rinan, had elephants.

ce314.text: He Zhuo wrote: with Jiaozhou, Sun Quan might send a giant elephant, but by then Cao Chong was long dead.

ce315.text: So He Zhuo said: this story was embellished. It's in the chapter-end notes of the Siku Quanshu edition of the Records.

ce316.text: That's what didn't fit: He Zhuo's years box in Chen Shou's missing one.

ce316b.text: Do the histories have any other elephant from Sun Quan to Cao Cao?

ce317.text: No. Odder: in all the Records, notes too, only Cao Chong's story has Sun Quan's elephant for Cao Cao.

ce318.text: Once Jiaozhou was Sun Quan's, it sent southern treasures yearly: pearls, tortoiseshell, rhino horn, ivory.

ce320.text: Run the numbers yourself and you'd likely land there too.

ce321.text: Another Qing scholar, Shao Jinhan, found a pig in a book's quote.

ce322.text: It's in an old book called the Fuzi.

ce323.text: A king was given a huge pig by a northerner; weighed on scale beams, it broke ten.

ce324.text: The result? In the end, he had the water official weigh it by boat: 1,000 jun.

ce325.text: The verdict: too big, no use.

ce326.text: I laugh at it every time.

ce327.text: Shao Jinhan said: weighing by boat existed well before Cao Chong.

ce329.text: The original is lost, and we couldn't verify its date;

ce330.text: it says by boat, but not how to mark or what to load.

ce331.text: He Zhuo had guessed too: the boat mark was probably a method already in some math book. Which, he didn't say.

ce332.text: If the story was embellished, where did the method come from?

ce401.text: From a Buddhist sutra. In 1930, the man who said so was Chen Yinke.

ce402.text: He said He Zhuo and Shao Jinhan never found a source.

ce403.text: That June's Tsinghua Journal ran it: four pages, a title pairing Cao Chong and Buddhist tales.

ce404.text: He opens: a few cases will prove it. Buddhist tales often crept into the Records' main text.

ce405.text: It's the Za Baozang Jing. Its Tale of the Land That Casts Out the Old also has someone weigh an elephant. Who?

ce406.text: Not a child: an old man hiding underground.

ce407.text: He lived in the Land That Casts Out the Old: by its law, all old people were sent far away.

ce408.text: His son, a minister, couldn't bear it. He dug a secret cellar, hid his father, and kept caring for him.

ce409.text: In his place, you'd probably do the same, right?

ce410.text: Here's the problem: later a deity set nine riddles.

ce411.text: The first two: tell a snake's sex, and who's asleep, who's awake.

ce412.text: The third: the deity asked how heavy this great white elephant was.

ce413.text: No minister at court knew, and a call across the kingdom found no one either.

ce413b.text: Note: in the sutra a deity sets this riddle; no one sends an elephant.

ce414.text: The minister went home to ask his father in the cellar. Did the old man say more?

ce415.text: He added two things: put the boat in a big pool;

ce416.text: load the same boat with stones; water at the line gives the weight.

ce417.text: The stones Chen Shou left out are in the sutra.

ce418.text: Did the stones in the version you remember come from here? We can't say, but they're here.

ce418b.text: The riddles only get stranger, up to "how is a handful of water more than the sea?"

ce419.text: All nine answered, the king decreed: stop casting out the old; care for them.

ce420.text: The tale ends: that old father was the Buddha in a past life.

ce421.text: It's about respecting elders, not smarts.

ce422.text: How did a tale of elder respect become Cao Chong's?

ce423.text: Chen Yinke held: elephants were southern, none in Cao Cao's land, so the tale used Sun Quan.

ce424.text: Typical of comparative folklore, he said.

ce425.text: He concluded: Cao Chong's story took in a Buddhist tale.

ce426.text: The Records came when Buddhism had just arrived, yet Indian tales had spread so far.

ce426b.text: So even Chen Shou's keen eye couldn't tell true from false.

ce427.text: Reading this, my first thought was: wait, when was this sutra translated into Chinese?

ce428.text: In 472, in the Northern Wei, two monks translated it.

ce429.text: Remember the year Chen Shou died? The sutra's translation came 175 years later.

ce430.text: That's odd. Yet Chen Yinke knew it himself, so he explained: this sutra was stitched together from others.

ce431.text: His example: another tale in it also appears in another translated sutra.

ce432.text: So maybe an earlier translation existed and was lost; or maybe it came to China by word of mouth and was pinned on Cao Chong.

ce433.text: But he couldn't produce a single earlier translation, nor did he say what that sutra was or where.

ce434.text: You may ask: what of the elephant? Could it not reach Cao Cao?

ce501.text: An elephant needed a sender; and while Cao Chong lived, Jiangdong sent tribute to the Han court.

ce503.text: and from 196 on, the court was in Cao Cao's hands.

ce504.text: That tribute really went to Cao Cao.

ce505.text: Think: wouldn't an elephant be the grandest goodwill gift?

ce506.text: But both sides were already wary: in 202, Cao Cao asked Sun Quan for a son as hostage, and Sun Quan refused.

ce507.text: If you were Sun Quan, withholding your son, would you send an elephant? It fits, and it doesn't.

ce508.text: Still, no record from those years mentions an elephant.

ce509.text: Was any elephant sent north by Sun Quan on record?

ce510.text: Yes. In 219, Sun Quan wrote Cao Cao as a subject, saying Cao Cao had Heaven's mandate.

ce511.text: Next year Cao Pi was emperor, Sun Quan a vassal; in Cao Pi's words, tribute "filled the roads."

ce513.text: Yes. Enter the letter from the start: the writer was Cao Pi, the recipient Wang Lang.

ce514.text: It says Sun Quan's envoys came again to submit: 100 baskets of pearls, 1,000 yi of gold, two tame elephants, male and female.

ce515.text: Plus tame parrots, and treasures by the boatload.

ce516.text: No year given. What's certain: by then Cao Chong had been dead over ten years. Was it Sun Quan's only elephant gift?

ce518.text: No. Encyclopedias: Zhuge Liang back in Chengdu from war, Sun Quan sent greetings, and Liu Shan two tame elephants.

ce518b.text: Lu Ji of Wu later lauded Sun Quan's era: foreign giant elephants and steeds in the stables.

ce519.text: And it wasn't the last: under the Jin, the court kept a tame elephant from the south, first in marshes by the water.

ce520.text: It got a cart and dozens of musicians; Nanyue men rode it, and each New Year court it was led into the hall.

ce521.text: So we think Chen Yinke went too far: elephants could reach the north.

ce523.text: Then, besides Chen Shou, did anyone else write about the weighing?

ce601.text: Yes. Yu Pu of the Jin. He wrote a book that has the weighing too.

ce602.text: It says: two tame elephants, Cao Chong "still young."

ce603.text: Versus Chen Shou, three changes: one elephant becomes two, "still young" is added, the "waterline" is gone. Still no number for Cao Chong's age.

ce604.text: Yu Pu died in Luoyang; his son crossed the Yangtze, gave it to Emperor Yuan; it was archived.

ce605.text: Did one book copy the other, or share a source?

ce607.text: What's sure: almost 200 years before the sutra's translation, two Jin men recorded it.

ce608.text: Today some scholars back Chen Yinke; others rebut him.

ce609.text: If you ask whose side I'm on: the archive's, and the archive stops here.

ce610.text: Remember our first question? Who first thought of the boat mark?

ce612.text: We think the same idea landed on a child in the histories, and on an old man in the sutra.

ce614.text: First met it in a textbook, storybook or cartoon? Tell me below.

ce615.text: This channel sticks to the record; subscribe to open files together.
